places.rationale: Strong growth momentum and a deep tech talent pool make 'better' the default, but extreme heat, near-maximal water stress and the nuclear rivalry with Pakistan keep a fat tail of decline and collapse.
Huge industrial and energy base and likely SI leadership favour gains, with automation offsetting extreme ageing; the main downside is a Taiwan or US-China war and a rigid political system.

Richest starting point, energy exporter and likely SI epicentre, so abundance is most reachable here, though high inequality makes the 9-in-10 bar hard; risks are great-power nuclear war, AI-driven power concentration and political breakdown.
Steady growth, energy and mineral self-sufficiency and a peaceful society support improvement; coastal subsidence, sea-level rise and weak water services are the main drags.

Very low political stability, Indus water dependence under heavy stress, extreme heat and floods, and a population heading toward half a billion make it one of the riskiest large countries, alongside nuclear rivalry with India.
Decades of flat per-capita income, oil dependence, insecurity and weak governance make long-run stagnation unusually likely, while ample water and a young workforce leave room for catch-up.

Abundant food, water and renewable energy and distance from great-power conflict limit collapse risk; the middle-income trap, violence and fiscal strain make stagnation the main alternative to improvement.

Impressive development record and good life expectancy point up, but one of the highest climate vulnerabilities (delta flooding, salinisation, cyclones), low readiness and political turbulence weigh heavily.
Energy wealth and low debt are offset by war, sanctions, shrinking population, hydrocarbon revenues eroded by the energy transition, a succession risk and its status as a prime nuclear target.
Rapid recent growth from a very low base and new hydropower favour improvement, but recurrent civil war, drought-driven famine risk and weak state capacity keep collapse risk high.
Integration with the US economy supports gains, while very high water stress, cartel violence and slow productivity growth make stagnation and decline real possibilities.

Superb state capacity, cohesion and robotics make it well placed to share SI gains broadly, but without SI three decades of flat consumption, extreme ageing, 205% debt and near-total energy and heavy food import dependence make stagnation likely.

Near-total dependence on a contested Nile, the world's largest wheat import bill, heavy debt service and a fast-growing population create serious decline and collapse risk; SI-cheapened desalination would help most.
Fast growth and a young population point up, but typhoons, sea-level rise, energy imports, South China Sea tension and an outsourcing economy exposed to automation add risk.

The weakest state capacity and adaptive readiness here, chronic conflict and a population set to roughly quadruple make it the most fragile case, though vast minerals, hydropower and water give real upside.
Strong, stable growth and high social cohesion favour improvement; the sinking, salinising Mekong delta and tensions with China are the main risks.
An educated population and energy wealth are undercut by aquifer depletion and acute water crisis, sanctions, regime instability and military confrontation with Israel and the US.

A diversified upper-middle-income economy with low public debt points up, but recurrent currency crises, 70% energy imports, rising water stress, fast ageing and a dangerous neighbourhood add downside.

A strong welfare state would spread SI gains broadly, but without SI ageing, 70% energy imports, industrial erosion and recent stagnation make flat consumption quite plausible; a Russia-NATO war is the collapse tail.
Thailand is ageing very fast before it gets rich, has slowing growth, recurring coups, high water stress and a flood-prone, sinking Bangkok, so stagnation is a substantial risk despite a solid base.
